Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

No. A virtual office is not accepted as the sole statutory seat. Article 9 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital (RDL 1/2010) requires the registered office to coincide with the place where the actual management is located or where the main establishment or operations are conducted. The nutraceuticals e-commerce license requires a physical address declared in the prior communication to the competent health authority and in the municipal trading license application; a virtual office can serve only as a supplementary correspondence address once a physical seat is registered and operational.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Central Commercial Registry (Registro Mercantil Central) for name reservation, and the competent Provincial Commercial Registry (Registro Mercantil Provincial) for inscription of the incorporation deed.

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010, of 2 July, approving the consolidated text of the Capital Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital), particularly articles 22 (minimum capital), 23 (public deed), 59 (registered office), 62 (subscription and payment of shares), 124-127 (bylaws) and 209-210 (board resolutions).

Formation / constitutional filings

Public deed of incorporation (escritura de constitución), submitted for legal inscription in the Provincial Commercial Registry and subsequent publication in the Official Gazette of the Commercial Registry (BORME).

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 25 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime Mandatory Capital Deposit & Lockup

For a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada, the minimum share capital is EUR 3,000, fully subscribed and paid up at incorporation. Cash contributions must be deposited in a Spanish credit institution in a blocked escrow-type account in the company's name; the bank certificate must be presented to the notary, and the deposit may be released only after the Mercantile Registry inscription is obtained.

Funding & unlock path: Fire-safety certification issued by the municipal fire service or an authorized inspection body, covering detection, extinguishing, and evacuation. Structural load inspections must be performed for storage racking and mezzanine areas. An occupational risk prevention assessment and plan must be prepared in accordance with Law 31/1995, including first-aid equipment, emergency coordination, and health surveillance when six or more workers are employed.

Paid-in capital rule: For a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada, the minimum share capital is EUR 3,000, fully subscribed and paid up at incorporation. Cash contributions must be deposited in a Spanish credit institution in a blocked escrow-type account in the company's name; the bank certificate must be presented to the notary, and the deposit may be released only after the Mercantile Registry inscription is obtained.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
RESOLVED FIRST: That the founding members approve the subscription and fully paid contribution of EUR 3,000 in cash, divided into 3,000 participating interests of EUR 1.00 each, evidenced by the bank deposit certificate issued by a Spanish credit institution. RESOLVED SECOND: That the statutory registered office is hereby fixed at [Madrid address], Calle ..., to serve as the principal place of administration, and the board may establish physical or logistical premises as business requires. RESOLVED THIRD: That [Full Name] is appointed Sole Administrator (Administrador Unico) with all powers permitted under the Capital Companies Act, and that execution of the public deed and all registry filings is ratified.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Mandatory Environmental Clearance

Spanish Agency for Medicines and Health Products (AEMPS) under the Ministry of Health; local competent authority (Ayuntamiento) for municipal activity and opening licensing.

Category: Prior communication for the placing on the market of food supplements (Comunicacion de puesta en el mercado de complementos alimenticios) and, where physical premises are used, the municipal Activity and Opening License or prior communication (Licencia de actividad y apertura / comunicacion previa de ejercicio).

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), including its Sede Electrónica at https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es. The AEAT administers Spanish corporate income tax, value added tax, tax identification numbers, the census of businesspersons and professionals, and VAT identification for intra-Community transactions. Customs matters are administered through the AEAT Customs and Excise Department.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada obtains its tax identification number (NIF) by filing Modelo 036 with the AEAT. A provisional NIF is generally requested after incorporation using the public deed or equivalent formation documentation, articles of association, registered office details, identification of directors and shareholders, and evidence of the company's incorporation process. The definitive NIF is obtained after registration with the Mercantile Registry and submission of the registered constitutional documents. The company must register in the Census of Entrepreneurs, Professionals and Withholding Agents before commencing taxable activity and must identify its economic activities and VAT obligations. The NIF normally serves as the Spanish VAT number; for intra-Community transactions and VIES purposes it is used with the prefix ES and requires registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios through Modelo 036. A foreign entity without a Spanish permanent establishment generally applies for a Spanish NIF through Modelo 036, directly or through an authorized representative, submitting its constitutional documents, foreign tax identification evidence, proof of authority, and Spanish translations and legalization or apostille where required. A non-established business seeking Spanish VAT registration must provide evidence of the taxable activities and appoint a Spanish tax representative where required by Spanish and EU VAT rules, particularly for businesses established outside the EU.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain has no U.S.-style check-the-box election for a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada. The SL is ordinarily subject to Spanish corporate income tax as a separate legal person. Available elections or optional regimes may include tax consolidation for qualifying corporate groups, the special regime for qualifying newly created entities or qualifying small entities where statutory conditions are met, the special regime for reorganizations, the patent box regime, and VAT special regimes where the business and transaction profile qualify. Spanish anti-hybrid-mismatch rules generally apply by operation of law and are not elective. VAT grouping, cash-accounting, and other special VAT regimes require statutory eligibility and timely election or notification.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general Spanish VAT turnover threshold applies. A person or entity carrying out an economic activity independently must register and comply with VAT from the commencement of taxable activity, subject to the applicable place-of-supply rules. The intra-Community VAT operator register has no general turnover threshold. Distance sales of goods to EU consumers are subject to the EU-wide EUR 10,000 threshold for the relevant combined intra-Community distance-sale and electronically supplied service rules, after which destination-country VAT generally applies; the One Stop Shop may be used where available. Spanish distance-selling and import rules may also require IOSS or destination-state registration depending on the transaction structure.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods from Spanish VAT territory to a destination outside the EU may qualify for VAT exemption with the right to deduct input VAT, provided the goods are dispatched or transported outside the EU and the supplier retains reliable evidence of export and exit. The supplier should normally be identified as exporter or otherwise prove the qualifying export transaction and link the customs exit evidence to the invoice and goods. Intra-Community supplies of goods may qualify for VAT exemption with the right to deduct input VAT where the customer is VAT-identified in another EU Member State, the goods are transported there, the supplier verifies and reports the customer's VAT number, and the required recapitulative statement and transport evidence are maintained. Services supplied to business customers established outside the relevant Spanish VAT territory may be outside the scope of Spanish VAT under the applicable place-of-supply rule, but the treatment depends on the service category, customer status, and use-and-enjoyment rules. Dietary supplements, nutraceuticals, medicines, and medical products must also satisfy applicable EU and Spanish product, labeling, health-claim, and market-placement requirements; tax treatment cannot be determined solely from the commercial description.

  • Electronic export declaration and customs Movement Reference Number (MRN), including evidence of customs release and exit from the EU customs territory
  • Commercial invoice and packing list identifying the supplier, consignee, goods, quantities, values, origin, and applicable tariff classification
  • Transport evidence, such as bill of lading, airway bill, courier manifest, or equivalent carrier record
  • Proof of delivery or destination, where necessary to establish that the goods left the EU and to link the shipment to the invoice
  • Exporter's EORI number and customs authorization or representation records, where applicable
  • For intra-Community supplies rather than third-country exports: customer's valid EU VAT number, transport evidence, and EC Sales List or equivalent recapitulative reporting
  • Accounting records linking the invoice, customs declaration, inventory movement, payment record, and VAT return
  • Bank payment or inward-remittance evidence where commercially available; Spanish VAT law does not impose a universal inward-remittance certificate as a condition for every export exemption

Spain does not currently impose universal real-time invoice clearance for all private-sector transactions. The Immediate Supply of Information system (Suministro Inmediato de Información, SII) requires near-real-time electronic submission of VAT invoice-record data, generally within four working days, for businesses with annual turnover exceeding EUR 6 million, VAT groups, entities registered in the monthly VAT refund regime, and businesses that voluntarily opt in. The electronic invoicing framework under Law 18/2022 on the Creation and Growth of Companies will require electronic invoicing for qualifying B2B transactions after its implementing rules and statutory transition periods become operative; consumer-facing obligations differ. The VERI*FACTU and related invoicing-system integrity rules require compliant software, traceability, integrity, retention, and, where applicable, secure transmission or reporting of invoice records under the applicable implementation timetable. There is no blanket requirement for a digital stamp or advance AEAT clearance on every invoice. Invoices must contain the required tax data, including supplier and customer identification, NIF where applicable, invoice number and date, taxable base, VAT rate, VAT amount, and legally required reverse-charge or exemption wording.

Spain has no general statutory 180-day foreign-exchange repatriation requirement for export proceeds. Export exemption depends principally on actual dispatch or transport outside the EU and adequate documentary proof, not on repatriation of sale proceeds within a fixed period. If an exemption or zero-rating claim is unsupported, the AEAT may assess the unpaid VAT, late-payment interest, and applicable penalties, and may deny or claw back input-VAT recovery connected with the transaction. Under the General Tax Law, penalties for incorrect tax treatment commonly range from 50% of the underpaid amount for ordinary infringements to 100% for serious infringements and up to 150% for very serious infringements, subject to statutory classifications, concealment, fraudulent means, repetition, and mitigation or reduction rules. False, manipulated, or deliberately incomplete customs evidence may also trigger customs debt, customs penalties, seizure or forfeiture consequences where applicable, and potentially criminal exposure for tax fraud or smuggling if statutory criminal thresholds and intent requirements are met. Refunds obtained without entitlement may be recovered with interest and sanctions. Documentation should be retained for the applicable Spanish tax limitation period, generally four years, without prejudice to longer retention periods applicable to customs, accounting, product-regulatory, or criminal matters.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain is a Eurozone member; the euro (EUR) is fully convertible for both current and capital account transactions. No exchange controls exist for residents or non-residents. Profit remittance is unrestricted, subject to standard corporate tax withholding (if applicable) and reporting to the Bank of Spain for statistical purposes. Capital account transactions (e.g., foreign direct investment, loans) require post-transaction declaration via the 'Declaración de Operaciones' (D-1, D-2, D-3 forms) but no prior authorization is needed.

Export proceeds surrender rules

No mandatory surrender or conversion of export proceeds is imposed. Exporters may retain foreign currency in domestic or foreign accounts. However, all export transactions exceeding €12,500 (or equivalent) must be reported to the Bank of Spain within 30 days of the transaction via the 'Declaración de Operaciones de Comercio Exterior' (D-1 form). No conversion ratio applies; proceeds can be held in EUR or foreign currency.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain) in coordination with the European Central Bank (ECB) for monetary policy and the Spanish Ministry of Economy for foreign exchange oversight

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Medium feasibility. Spain licenses Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs) under the PSD2 framework (e.g., Bnext, Monei, or foreign EMIs with passporting rights). However, for high-risk nutraceutical e-commerce, EMIs often impose stricter due diligence and may decline due to the sector's AML risk. Legal constraints include the need for a Spanish or EU passporting license, and EMIs typically do not provide credit facilities or complex FX hedging. They are viable for operational accounts but not for capital escrow or large trade settlements.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

High-risk industry classification (ISIC 4791 – online retail of dietary supplements) triggers enhanced due diligence (EDD) under Spanish AML Law 10/2010.

Root cause: High-risk industry classification (ISIC 4791 – online retail of dietary supplements) triggers enhanced due diligence (EDD) under Spanish AML Law 10/2010.

Defense evidence: Provide: (1) Valid pharmaceutical/nutraceutical license from the Spanish Agency for Medicines and Health Products (AEMPS) or regional authority; (2) Certificate of incorporation and tax ID (NIF); (3) Detailed business plan and source of funds declaration; (4) Beneficial ownership register (Registro de Titularidades Reales); (5) Compliance manual and AML training certificates; (6) Bank references from previous financial institutions; (7) Audited financial statements (if available).
Cross-border transactions to/from high-risk jurisdictions (e.g., Latin America) may trigger sanctions screening and PEP checks.

Root cause: Cross-border transactions to/from high-risk jurisdictions (e.g., Latin America) may trigger sanctions screening and PEP checks.

Defense evidence: Provide: (1) Commercial contracts and invoices with clear purpose codes; (2) Export/import documentation (customs declarations, bills of lading); (3) Proof of regulatory compliance in target markets (e.g., FDA, ANVISA); (4) Detailed transaction flow chart; (5) Legal opinion on sanctions exposure; (6) Enhanced due diligence on counterparties.
Unclear source of initial capital injection (minimum capital for SL is €3,000, but higher amounts may be scrutinized).

Root cause: Unclear source of initial capital injection (minimum capital for SL is €3,000, but higher amounts may be scrutinized).

Defense evidence: Provide: (1) Bank statements showing the origin of funds; (2) Notarized declaration of source of wealth; (3) Tax clearance certificate (AEAT); (4) Proof of transfer from shareholders' personal accounts; (5) If funds from foreign investors, provide foreign exchange transaction records and declaration to Bank of Spain.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Compliant wire transfer via SWIFT MT103 with purpose code 'G300' (equity injection) or 'G100' (direct investment). The transfer must be accompanied by a notarized capital increase resolution and filed with the Commercial Registry. For amounts above €1,000,000, a prior declaration to the Bank of Spain (D-2 form) is required. Verification includes matching the beneficiary name (SL) and NIF, and ensuring the sender is the shareholder. For non-EU transfers, additional anti-money laundering checks apply.Clearing rails for trade settlements: (1) SWIFT MT103 for direct wire transfers to suppliers, with purpose code 'G200' (trade payments) or 'G300' (imports). (2) Commercial Letters of Credit (LC) via SWIFT MT700 for large or recurring purchases, especially from Asia or Latin America. (3) For intra-EU payments, SEPA Instant Credit Transfer (SCT Inst) is available for low-value transactions. All outbound payments must be reported to the Bank of Spain if exceeding €12,500 (D-1 form).FX Forward Contracts (deliverable) – available for EUR/USD, EUR/GBP, and other major pairs; requires a credit line with the bank.Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) – permissible for exotic currencies (e.g., BRL, MXN) where deliverable forwards are illiquid; typically offered by larger banks.Currency Swaps – for long-term hedging of cross-border cash flows, subject to ISDA agreements and collateral requirements.FX Options – available for strategic hedging, but require premium payment and are less common for SMEs.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium feasibility. Spain licenses Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs) under the PSD2 framework (e.g., Bnext, Monei, or foreign EMIs with passporting rights). However, for high-risk nutraceutical e-commerce, EMIs often impose stricter due diligence and may decline due to the sector's AML risk. Legal constraints include the need for a Spanish or EU passporting license, and EMIs typically do not provide credit facilities or complex FX hedging. They are viable for operational accounts but not for capital escrow or large trade settlements.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general Corporate Income Tax rate for Spanish-resident companies, including an Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL). The rate is subject to statutory reduced-rate regimes applicable by tax year and taxpayer profile.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax generally applies to dividends paid by a Spanish company to non-residents. Domestic exemptions may apply, including the EU Parent-Subsidiary regime where the recipient and payer satisfy ownership, holding-period, subject-to-tax, legal-form, beneficial-ownership, anti-abuse, and anti-hybrid requirements. A tax treaty may reduce the rate, commonly to 5%, 10%, or 15%, depending on the treaty and participation conditions.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Modelo 200: within 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year company ending on 31 December, the usual filing window is 1 to 25 July of the following year. Modelo 202: generally 1 to 20 April, October, and December, with electronic direct-debit cut-off dates usually earlier. Modelo 232: generally within the month following the ten months after the end of the tax period; for a 31 December year-end, ordinarily 1 to 30 November of the following year.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally filed and paid from the first day through the twentieth day of April, October, and December. The payment deadline may be earlier when using direct debit.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally within the month following the ten months after the end of the tax period.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: There is no single monetary threshold that universally triggers all Spanish Local File and Master File obligations. A Local File is generally required for material related-party transactions, subject to statutory exemptions for certain entities and transaction categories. The principal safe-harbor threshold for not preparing related-party documentation is generally transactions with the same related party not exceeding EUR 250,000 in aggregate at arm's-length value during the tax period, subject to important exclusions and transaction-specific rules. Modelo 232 reporting may be triggered at EUR 250,000 for transactions of the same type and valuation method with the same related party, or by separate percentage and special-regime thresholds. Master File obligations generally apply to entities forming part of a qualifying multinational group, subject to statutory exemptions and size thresholds. Large multinational groups may also have Country-by-Country Reporting obligations, generally at the EUR 750 million consolidated revenue threshold.

Economic substance scope: Spain has no standalone economic-substance regulation identical to the UAE or certain other ESR regimes. Nevertheless, substance is material under Spanish anti-abuse rules, the Principal Purpose Test in applicable treaties, beneficial-ownership requirements, the EU Parent-Subsidiary and Interest and Royalties Directives, controlled foreign company rules, hybrid mismatch rules, permanent-establishment principles, and general anti-avoidance provisions. A Spanish SL should maintain real decision-making, adequate personnel or outsourced operational capacity, premises or operational infrastructure, commercial risk, books and records, local management control, and evidence that cross-border arrangements have genuine business purposes. A letterbox company, conduit dividend vehicle, artificial service provider, or entity lacking control over risks may lose treaty or directive benefits and face reassessment.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate Income Tax evasion and concealed revenue

Statutory sanction: Tax assessment, late-payment interest, and a tax penalty generally ranging from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax depending on concealment, fraud, repetition, and cooperation. Serious tax fraud exceeding EUR 120,000 per tax period may constitute a criminal offense; aggravated fraud exceeding EUR 600,000 or involving an organization or particularly serious circumstances may attract substantially higher imprisonment and fines.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may incur civil liability for unpaid taxes where they caused or failed to prevent the infringement, and criminal liability where they participated knowingly. Criminal tax convictions may result in imprisonment, fines, disqualification from public benefits or subsidies, and seizure or confiscation of assets. Travel restrictions may be imposed in criminal or enforcement proceedings where legally justified; they are not automatic for every tax debt.
VAT fraud and carousel or missing-trader arrangements

Statutory sanction: Repayment of unduly claimed VAT, interest, administrative penalties commonly linked to the unpaid or improperly claimed amount, and possible criminal prosecution for serious VAT fraud. Customs duties, import VAT, seizure, and product-related penalties may also apply.

Director personal liability: Directors who knowingly approve false VAT chains or benefit from fraudulent refunds may face joint liability, criminal prosecution, imprisonment, fines, asset seizure, and disqualification. Lack of knowledge is not a defense where governance failures amount to willful blindness.
Withholding-tax non-compliance

Statutory sanction: Assessment of the unwithheld tax, late-payment interest, filing and payment penalties, and potential liability for the payer as withholding agent. Incorrect treaty application may also trigger interest and anti-abuse reassessment.

Director personal liability: Directors may be secondarily liable where the company deliberately or negligently failed to withhold or remit tax. Intentional concealment or falsification may create criminal exposure.
Transfer-pricing manipulation

Statutory sanction: Primary adjustment to taxable income, secondary adjustment, withholding consequences, interest, documentation penalties, and transfer-pricing penalties. Failure to provide documentation can generate fixed penalties and percentage-based penalties linked to the adjustment or omitted data.

Director personal liability: Directors may face civil liability for knowingly approving non-arm's-length arrangements and criminal liability if the arrangements are part of deliberate tax fraud. Liability is not created solely by an unfavorable pricing outcome where contemporaneous support and reasonable methodology exist.
Shell company, treaty shopping, and beneficial-ownership abuse

Statutory sanction: Denial of treaty or directive relief, withholding at the domestic rate, tax assessment, interest, anti-avoidance penalties, and possible recharacterization of payments or transactions under Spanish and treaty anti-abuse rules.

Director personal liability: Directors and controlling persons may incur civil liability and, where fraud is intentional, criminal liability. Corporate separateness may be disregarded in exceptional cases of abuse, asset commingling, fraudulent undercapitalization, or use of the company to defeat creditors.
Anti-money laundering and terrorist-financing exposure

Statutory sanction: Spanish AML penalties may be classified as minor, serious, or very serious, with substantial administrative fines, public statements, temporary restrictions, and possible loss of authorization. Criminal money-laundering conduct may result in imprisonment, fines, and confiscation.

Director personal liability: Directors, compliance officers, and beneficial owners may be personally fined or prosecuted where they knowingly participate, consent, or negligently permit AML breaches. Asset freezing and travel restrictions may arise in criminal investigations or judicial proceedings.
Pharmaceutical, food-supplement, and product-safety violations

Statutory sanction: Administrative fines, product withdrawal, recall, seizure, closure, suspension or loss of authorization, customs detention, consumer claims, and possible criminal liability for public-health offenses, fraud, or counterfeit products.

Director personal liability: Directors and responsible officers may face personal fines, civil compensation, professional disqualification, and imprisonment for intentional or grossly negligent conduct causing public-health harm. Corporate insurance may not cover deliberate regulatory violations.
Customs and import misclassification

Statutory sanction: Recovery of customs duties and import VAT, customs penalties, seizure or forfeiture, loss of simplified procedures, and potential anti-fraud prosecution.

Director personal liability: Directors may be jointly liable under customs and tax provisions where they directed or knowingly tolerated false declarations. Criminal liability may arise for organized or fraudulent evasion.
Accounting, corporate-law, and insolvency misconduct

Statutory sanction: Restitution of unlawful dividends, civil damages, director disqualification, insolvency clawback, creditor claims, accounting penalties, and possible criminal sanctions for false accounting or insolvency offenses.

Director personal liability: Directors may be ordered to cover all or part of the insolvency shortfall, compensate creditors, return diverted assets, and bear litigation costs. Criminal offenses may result in imprisonment, fines, and disqualification from management.
Electronic commerce and consumer-protection non-compliance

Statutory sanction: Consumer, e-commerce, data-protection, and advertising fines; injunctions; refund and compensation claims; suspension of campaigns; and potential restrictions on processing or selling products.

Director personal liability: Directors may be personally liable for deliberate or grossly negligent violations, especially where they approve misleading health claims, conceal the seller's identity, or disregard repeated regulator notices.
